title: Inventory and Your First Command
objective: Understand Ansible's control-node model and describe a managed host in YAML inventory.

sourceAlignment.title: Ansible for DevOps, 2nd Edition
sourceAlignment.author: Jeff Geerling
sourceAlignment.note: Original Code Forge lesson aligned to the chapter's concepts; no book prose is reproduced. Browser exercises validate YAML locally and never contact infrastructure.

paragraphs: Ansible automates remote systems from a control node. You describe the state you want, and Ansible connects to managed nodes—usually over SSH—to inspect them and apply only the changes they need.

An inventory answers the first practical question: which machines should Ansible manage? Hosts can stand alone or belong to groups such as webservers and databases. Grouping lets one command or play target a useful slice of your infrastructure.

Modern inventories can be written in YAML. The top-level all group can contain children, each child group can contain hosts, and host variables such as ansible_host can record the address Ansible should connect to.

Ansible is designed around idempotence: running a well-written task again should leave an already-correct system unchanged. That makes automation repeatable instead of turning every rerun into a risky special event.
explanation.rule: Keep inventory focused on hosts and connection data; put the desired configuration in playbooks.

examples.title: A Small YAML Inventory
examples.code:
all:
  children:
    webservers:
      hosts:
        web01:
          ansible_host: 192.0.2.10
examples.note: 192.0.2.0/24 is reserved for documentation, so this example cannot accidentally identify a real public server.

examples.title: Target the Group
examples.note: The ping module checks whether Ansible can connect and run Python on each target; it is not an ICMP network ping.

checks.question: What is the main purpose of an Ansible inventory?
options: To list managed hosts and organize them into targetable groups.
To install Ansible on every managed host.
To store the output of every playbook run.
To replace SSH with a proprietary agent.

feedback.correct: Correct—the inventory defines the systems and groups Ansible can target.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. Inventory describes managed hosts and their grouping; it is not an installer, log, or agent.

checks.question: What should happen when an idempotent task runs against a system that is already in the desired state?
options: It should make no unnecessary change.
It should rebuild the system from scratch.
It should always report a fatal error.
It should remove the host from inventory.

feedback.correct: Exactly. The desired state is already satisfied, so no change is needed.
feedback.incorrect: Idempotence means repeated runs converge on the same desired state without needless changes.

assignment.title: Register the First Web Server
assignment.brief: Complete a YAML inventory with a webservers group containing web01 at the documentation address 192.0.2.10.
requirements: Define the top-level all group and a children mapping.
Create a webservers group with a hosts mapping.
Add web01 with ansible_host set to 192.0.2.10.
Use spaces, not tabs, and two-space indentation.
assignment.starterCode:
all:
  children:
    # Add the webservers group and its host here.
assignment.solutionCode:
all:
  children:
    webservers:
      hosts:
        web01:
          ansible_host: 192.0.2.10
assignment.outputCheckLabel: Inventory uses valid course-style YAML structure

hints: Nest webservers two spaces beneath children.
Nest hosts beneath webservers, then web01 beneath hosts.
Host variables go beneath the hostname: ansible_host: 192.0.2.10.
